AMD rides data center riches to ‘largest and most profitable’ quarter in history

By Kamali

AMD posted record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier, driven by a 97% jump in data center sales to $8.5 billion. The chipmaker forecast about $17 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter, well above what analysts had expected, though its gaming business shrank and cash flow weakened.

AMD has reported the biggest quarter in its history, with demand for artificial intelligence hardware pushing its data center business to nearly double in a year. The chipmaker released its third-quarter 2026 results on November 3, covering the period that ended September 26. CEO Lisa Su described the quarter on the earnings call as the largest and most profitable in the company's history.

The headline numbers

Revenue came in at $13.4 billion, up 45% from $9.2 billion a year earlier and up 16% from the previous quarter. That was above the top of AMD's own forecast range of $12.7 billion to $13.3 billion, and above the roughly $13.1 billion that analysts had expected, according to figures cited by Shacknews and The Next Web.

Profit rose even faster than sales. On a GAAP basis, net income was $2.4 billion, or $1.46 per diluted share, up from $0.75 a year ago. Excluding items such as stock-based compensation, earnings per share were $2.09, up 74%. Gross margin was 54% on a GAAP basis and 56% on a non-GAAP basis.

Data center drives the results

The data center segment generated $8.5 billion in revenue, up 97% from $4.3 billion a year earlier. It now accounts for about 64% of AMD's total revenue, compared with 47% a year ago. Operating income in the segment reached about $2.9 billion, up from $1.1 billion. AMD credited strong demand for its EPYC server processors and the launch of its Instinct MI450 series of AI accelerator chips.

Other parts of the business did less well. Client and Gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Within that segment, sales of client processors rose 7% to about $2.95 billion on demand for Ryzen laptop chips, while gaming revenue dropped 40% to $773 million because of lower sales of custom chips and graphics products. Embedded revenue grew 29% to $1.1 billion.

What AMD expects next

AMD guided for fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion. That implies growth of roughly 66% from a year earlier and about 27% from the third quarter, and it is above the $16.2 billion that analysts had forecast. Su said she expects growth to accelerate as AMD scales up production of its Helios rack-scale systems and its next-generation Venice server processors. She also told analysts she expects revenue to grow by more than 80% in 2027, with data center as the largest contributor.

Shares rose more than 5% in after-hours trading following the report.

Where the cautions are

The strong income statement was not matched by cash flow. Reports on the results say free cash flow fell by almost two-thirds, with inventory building and capital spending weighing on cash conversion. That is common for a company ramping up production of complex new products, but it is something investors will watch.

There is also a concentration risk. With data center sales supplying nearly two-thirds of revenue, AMD's fortunes are tied closely to how long the AI infrastructure spending boom continues at its current pace. The company's gaming business, once a main pillar, is shrinking.

What is still unknown

The guidance is AMD's own forecast and not a result, and it depends on the new products reaching volume production on schedule. It is not yet clear how the company's margins will develop as the Instinct and Helios systems scale, or how much of the demand comes from a small number of very large AI customers.

Why it matters

AMD is the main challenger to Nvidia in AI chips, and these results show it winning a growing share of the money companies are spending on AI data centers. For the wider industry, the numbers are another sign that demand for AI computing capacity remains strong, even after a recent period of nervousness in chip stocks. For AMD, the next few quarters will test whether it can turn rapid revenue growth into steady profits and cash.
